title: Death and dying, closed
hook: certain, uncertain, and the practice that helps
tomorrow: what happens when you get what you want, and when you don't?

segments.voice: Yesterday, living because of death: those who know we all come to an end let their quarrels go. Love now. And a question: what can anyone know for sure?
screen: `LOVE NOW.` → `WHAT CAN YOU KNOW FOR SURE?`

segments.voice: Ask a table of friends what happens after we die, and the debate starts before the food arrives. Somebody is sure. Somebody laughs it off. Somebody goes quiet. An old story puts that whole table into four short answers, given by a weaver's daughter to the Buddha in front of a crowd. And the crowd thinks she's being rude.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER WE DIE?` → `A WEAVER'S DAUGHTER, FOUR ANSWERS.` → `THE CROWD THINKS SHE'S RUDE.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Dhammapada commentary. In the town of Alavi, the Buddha had taught a simple reflection: my life is uncertain, my death is certain. Later he asks the girl four questions. Where have you come from? I don't know. Where are you going? I don't know. Don't you know? I know. Do you know? I don't know. People mutter. Then she explains. I don't know where I was before this birth. I don't know where I'll go after it. I know I will die. I don't know when. The Buddha praises every answer. The commentary adds a hard ending: later that day, at her father's loom, she dies in an accident. Certain, and uncertain. Now the debate, because Buddhists read the unknown part in more than one way. Some say rebirth and kamma are plainly part of the teaching. Their best case: she didn't doubt that she was going somewhere, only where, and that long view is what makes each act matter. Others lean on a sutta where the Buddha speaks to the Kalamas, townspeople unsure whom to trust. Their best case: he offers assurances for both possibilities. If there is a next life and deeds bear fruit, a kind life goes well. If there isn't, a person free of hatred lives at ease here and now. Practice doesn't wait for certainty. Notice where the two sides meet. Neither says the time is known. Both send you back to the same place: this life, now.
screen: `MY DEATH IS CERTAIN.` · `I KNOW I WILL DIE. NOT WHEN.` · `REBIRTH IS THE LONG VIEW.` · `KALAMAS: GOOD EITHER WAY.` · then, large: `THIS LIFE, NOW.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand open on your knee. With each slow breath, fold in one finger for one plain gift this life gave you today: a meal, a voice, warm water, light through a window. When the hand is closed, open it again and keep counting until the bell.
Death and dying: a whole block on the one thing that's certain and the many that aren't. The block closes on a girl's honest answers.
Keep this one: this life, now, and the rest can stay an open question. Death and dying, closed.

howItsDone: The weaver's daughter's story is told in Theravada teaching on reflection on death, with the line 'life is uncertain, death is certain'; Buddhists of different schools hold rebirth with different emphasis, and teachers sometimes cite the Kalama Sutta's assurances for those still unsure.

fork.setup: a friend says rebirth is the whole point of the path. you lean toward the Kalama assurances. what's her best case, in her own terms?
options: she knows she's going somewhere, so every act has a long reach.
rebirth is comforting, so it helps people stop worrying.
the Buddha never mentioned rebirth, so she's adding it in.
fork.reveal: the weaver's daughter doubted only where she'd go, not whether. for those who hold rebirth plainly, that long view is what gives each act weight. the Kalama side has its own best case: practice doesn't wait for certainty.

original.note: Pali: death. In the reflection: life uncertain, maraṇa certain.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists all agree on exactly what happens after death.
what it means: one thing is certain, death; its time is not. Buddhists hold the after-question with different emphasis, and meet in this life, now.
what a scholar hears: the weaver's daughter is in the Dhammapada commentary on verse 174; the both-ways assurances are in AN 3.65, the Kalama Sutta.

chat.says: got into a summer art program 😳 far away. but ông's old. what if something happens while i'm gone?
options: nobody knows when, at home or away. talk to ông, then choose this life.
then stay home. if you're right there, you can't be caught off guard.
just go and don't think about it. worrying about death is pointless.
chat.meaning: The weaver's daughter knew death is certain and its time unknown. Staying home can't buy certainty; the honest move is this life, now.

tie.story: The weaver's daughter told the Buddha: I know I will die; I don't know when.
tie.friend: Mai can't control when Ông's time comes, home or away; she can talk with him and choose this summer honestly.
tie.you: what are you putting off until you feel sure?

Alavi.meaning: the town where, in the story, the Buddha taught the reflection

kamma.meaning: intentional action and its results; Sanskrit karma

Kalamas.meaning: townspeople who asked the Buddha whom to trust

Dhammapada.meaning: an old collection of the Buddha's verses

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary (Dhammapada-atthakatha) on verse 174: the weaver's daughter of Alavi
Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kalama Sutta: the assurances, whether or not there is another world)

notes: Weaver's daughter paraphrased from the Dhammapada commentary on verse 174 (the four questions and answers; the crowd's displeasure; the Buddha's praise; her death at the loom later that day). The commentary also gives her age and the years she practiced; left out on purpose (claims rule). The reflection 'my life is uncertain, my death is certain' is the commentary's; confirm wording.
Gentle note for parents: the story ends with the girl's accidental death at her father's loom; told in one line, without detail.

Debate shape: the two views are (1) rebirth and kamma held as plainly taught, and (2) practicing with the Kalama Sutta's assurances (AN 3.65) without settling the question. Confirm both are stated fairly and neither is ranked; the Kalama assurances are paraphrased (the sutta gives them in a fuller form).
Fork's wrong option 'the Buddha never mentioned rebirth' is presented as a mistake a skimmer might make; it is false to the suttas.
